finding.title: UnixFileLock follows a symlink at the lock path and truncates its target
finding.evidence: In filelock/_unix.py, UnixFileLock._acquire computes open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (line 41), adds O_CREAT only when Path(self.lock_file).exists() is false (lines 42-43), then calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) at line 44. No O_NOFOLLOW is ever added (contrast the hardened sibling implementation, which does add getattr(os,'O_NOFOLLOW') there). Because O_TRUNC is unconditionally present, when the lock path already exists as a symlink to another file the kernel follows the link and truncates the link target to zero bytes. The lock_file is a caller-supplied path (FileLockMeta.__call__ / BaseFileLock.__init__ -> os.fspath(lock_file) at _api.py line 184), so a lock path in a directory an attacker can write (shared /tmp-style or project working directory) can be replaced by a symlink. When the victim process then acquires its lock, an arbitrary file writable by the victim (e.g. the victim user's config, database or secret file) is silently truncated, destroying its contents (integrity/availability). Path exists()/os.open being separate calls also yields a TOCTOU window even with the O_CREAT branch. A local PoC harness replicating the exact flags (os.open(lock, O_RDWR|O_TRUNC, 0o644) with a symlink planted at lock) was prepared but the execution call was cut off by the call budget before producing output; the source-level flow above is directly inspected and unambiguous. Protection gap: unlike _util.raise_on_not_writable_file, which was rewritten to use lstat specifically to defeat hostile symlinks, _unix.py still opens with a following, truncating open, so the mitigating intent is not applied at the actual unsafe operation.

review_queue.evidence: os.open at line 44 follows the attacker-controlled lock path with O_TRUNC set at line 41 and no O_NOFOLLOW; same protected-file truncation root cause one line after the expected sink. Directory write access and victim write permission are prerequisites.

finding.title: Empty/null verification key disables signature requirement, allowing unsigned token forgery
finding.evidence: Attacker-controlled token header/payload flows into verify() -> verifyToken() (verifier.js:173). The key presence guard at line 180 computes `const hasKey = key instanceof Buffer ? key.length : !!key`, so a caller-configured empty string or null key yields hasKey=false. The branch at verifier.js:182 then does NOT raise `missingSignature` (only the `hasKey && !signature` case does), and validateAlgorithmAndSignature (line 188) only calls verifySignature when a signature is truthy (src/crypto.js path reached from verifier.js:139). An unsigned token (`header.payload.` with alg HS256 as configured) therefore skips all cryptographic verification. Executed PoC (node poc_run.js in an isolated copy of this source) reproduced: key="" algorithms=[HS256], UNSIGNED token => ACCEPTED {"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}; key=null likewise ACCEPTED, while the control key="secret" correctly rejected with FAST_JWT_MISSING_SIGNATURE. Root cause is that key absence is treated as 'no signature required' instead of 'reject', so any deployment that passes an empty/missing secret (common with env-var config) accepts fully forged tokens.

review_queue.evidence: verifyToken rejects a missing signature only when the key is truthy; key:null with algorithms:['HS256'] accepts an HS256 header with an empty signature. round4-jwt-verification.json confirms real-key and async-null-key paths reject. Conditional on an invalid key configuration, not a bypass of a correctly keyed verifier.

finding.title: Asymmetric public key misclassified as HMAC secret (algorithm confusion)
finding.evidence: When callers pass allowedAlgorithms=[HS256] plus a PEM/JWK public key, verifier.js createVerifier (line 401) calls detectPublicKeyAlgorithms, which reaches performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms (src/crypto.js:125). Detection anchors its regexes at position 0 and never trims or locates the PEM block: `key.match(publicKeyPemMatcher)` at line 126 fails for a key with any leading byte (whitespace, BOM, zero-width char, wrapper comment), and the raw-JWK/JSON branch falls through to the `return hsAlgorithms` fallback at line 135. The public key bytes are then passed to verifySignature as an HMAC secret. Because RSA/EC/OKP public keys and serialized JWK JSON are public by design, an attacker who knows the verification key can compute the same HMAC and forge an HS256 token. Executed PoC reproduced: leading-space PEM algorithms=[HS256], forged HS256 => ACCEPTED {"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}; raw JWK JSON algorithms=[HS256], forged HS256 => ACCEPTED; control with a normally-formatted PEM rejected as FAST_JWT_INVALID_KEY. Root cause is non-normalized key-shape detection combined with a silent fallback to symmetric algorithms.

review_queue.evidence: PEM-detection matcher in the algorithm-confusion family; not reproduced this round.

finding.title: Unbounded BLAKE2b key length overflows 128-byte stack buffer
finding.evidence: blake2b() passes the caller-supplied key straight through: line 281 `crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), msg, len(msg))` (the same unvalidated sink is reachable from the Blake2b class at line 297 `crypto_blake2b_keyed_init(&self._ctx, self._hash_size, key, len(key))`). No length check exists on `key` anywhere in the binding. In monocypher.c crypto_blake2b_keyed_init does `u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);` and COPY is `FOR(_i_,0,size) dst[_i_]=src[_i_]`, so any `key` longer than 128 bytes copies len(key) bytes from the Python buffer into the 128-byte stack array. Input such as `blake2b(b'x', key=b'A'*1000)` or `Blake2b(key=b'A'*1000)` is a fully attacker-controlled stack buffer overflow (attacker-chosen length and contents) with no intervening validation, yielding memory corruption/RCE in the host process.

review_queue.evidence: blake2b passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed; monocypher.c copies key_size bytes into key_block[128]. Keys >128 bytes overflow the stack. Source-verified; remote reachability is not claimed.

finding.title: argon2i_32 lacks nb_blocks minimum check, causing heap buffer overflow/OOB
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 accepts `nb_blocks` directly from the caller and only sizes the work area as `malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * 1024)` (line 345) before calling `crypto_argon2(...)` (line 347); it never enforces the documented Monocypher requirement (monocypher.h line 160: `nb_blocks; // memory hardness, >= 8 * nb_lanes`). In monocypher.c crypto_argon2 computes `segment_size = nb_blocks/1/4`, `lane_size = segment_size*4`, and always writes the first two 1024-byte blocks for lane 0 (`blocks[l*lane_size + i]`, i=0,1). With nb_blocks=1, segment_size=lane_size=0, so the code writes blocks[0] and blocks[1] into a 1024-byte allocation (1 KB heap overflow); with nb_blocks=0, malloc(0) is written past/HIT, and `last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1` becomes blocks-1, an out-of-bounds heap read later serialized into the hash output. Callers passing user-controlled cost parameters (e.g. `argon2i_32(1, 3, password, salt)`) can therefore corrupt or leak heap memory.

review_queue.evidence: Unvalidated nb_blocks sizes the work area while native Argon2 reads initialized blocks; same expected undersized-work-area root cause with an alternate CWE at the expected line.

finding.title: Missing key/nonce length validation causes out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: lock/unlock (lines 181/199), chacha20 (lines 267/269), key_exchange (line 375), compute_key_exchange_public_key (line 362) and signature_check (line 429) forward caller keys/nonces/public keys/signatures of arbitrary length to the C API without length checks (only IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption and the elligator functions validate). The C layer unconditionally reads fixed sizes: crypto_aead_init_x calls crypto_chacha20_h which reads key[32] and nonce[16], then `COPY(ctx->nonce, nonce+16, 8)` reads nonce[16..23]; crypto_aead_unlock reads mac[16]; crypto_chacha20_djb/ietf read key[32] plus nonce[8]/[12]; crypto_eddsa_check reads signature[64]/public_key[32]. Passing shorter objects (e.g. `lock(b'k', b'n', b'msg')` or `chacha20(b'shortkey', b'0'*24, b'data')`) makes the library read bytes beyond the Python buffer; the resulting keystream/derived values depend on adjacent heap contents, so an attacker able to supply wrong-sized crypto material and observe the output can leak process memory.

review_queue.evidence: lock()/unlock() pass caller-controlled key and nonce buffers into native routines declaring key[32]/nonce[24] without a length check; the incremental wrapper guards lengths at lines 214-218. Distinct AEAD bounds defect; no native crash or disclosure reproduced.

finding.title: Double-drop of elements when an element's Drop panics in ThinVec::clear
finding.evidence: ThinVec::clear (src/lib.rs:1082-1087) calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` and then `self.set_len(0)`. The length is only reset AFTER all element destructors run, with no unwind guard. If an element in the middle of the buffer panics during its Drop, unwinding leaves the header length unchanged, so the surviving `ThinVec` still reports the original `len` and its Drop impl (line 1917) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` over the whole range again. Elements [0..i] (already dropped before the panicking one) are dropped a second time, a double-drop/use-after-free of a value the attacker controls, and allocator metadata may be deallocated twice if the second destructor frees. Realistic prerequisite: attacker-supplied element type implementing a panicking Drop (or a `catch_unwind`ed panic path), plus length >= 2 so at least one prior element exists. The fix is absent here: thin-vec 0.2.16 replaces this exact sequence with a DropGuard that resets the length during unwinding (comment 'Decrement len even in the case of a panic.') and adds regression test `test_panic_clear`.

review_queue.evidence: clear sets len to zero only after drop_in_place; a destructor panic leaves the stale length. Same panic-safety root cause one line after the expected sink.

finding.title: Double-drop in IntoIter::drop when an element destructor panics mid-drop
finding.evidence: IntoIter::drop (src/lib.rs:2539-2555) performs `let mut vec = mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new()); ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..]); vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (lines 2546-2548). If a destructor in the `[start..]` range panics, `set_len_non_singleton(0)` is never reached and `vec` is dropped during unwinding with its length still equal to its original value, so `ThinVec::drop`/`drop_non_singleton` (line 1917) re-runs `drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` over the entire range. Elements already dropped before the panicking one, and elements that `next()` already moved out (which `start` was supposed to exclude), are dropped again: a double-drop of attacker-influenced values reachable whenever the iterator's `Drop` runs during unwinding. The fix is absent here: thin-vec 0.2.16 adds a DropGuard in this scope with the comment 'Leak on panic.' that resets the length via `set_len_non_singleton(0)` during unwinding, plus regression test `test_panic_into_iter`, confirming the guard is required to prevent this double-drop.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop length reset after drop_in_place; same panic-safety root cause as the expected line-2546 sink.

finding.title: Asymmetric key material misclassified as an HMAC secret enables algorithm confusion / token forgery
finding.evidence: performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms classifies the configured verification key using the ^-anchored matchers privateKeyPemMatcher/publicKeyPemMatcher (src/crypto.js:26-27, 126-128). Because these regexes are anchored without /m, any leading byte (whitespace, control char, zero-width unicode, a wrapper/comment before the block) makes the match fail, so the PEM/X509 tests at lines 126-141 do not fire and execution falls through to line 133-135 (`if (!publicKeyPemMatch && !key.includes(publicKeyX509CertMatcher)) return hsAlgorithms`). The same fall-through happens for any non-PEM asymmetric key material, e.g. a serialized public JWK (`{"kty":"RSA",...}`) or a JWKS array, which also has no PEM header. The misclassification propagates: createVerifier sets allowedAlgorithms to the returned hsAlgorithms (src/verifier.js:401-407) and prepareKeyOrSecret treats the public key string as a symmetric secret because availableAlgorithms[0] === hsAlgorithms[0] (src/verifier.js:409). An attacker who knows the public key (it is public) can therefore compute an HS256/384/512 HMAC using the full key string (including the leading bytes) as the secret and submit a forged JWT. validateAlgorithmAndSignature accepts it because header.alg 'HS256' is in the hs allowlist (src/verifier.js:134) and it is verified with the same secret (src/crypto.js:282-287), yielding a full authentication/signature bypass. The later hardened release replaced the anchored matchers with an unanchored pemBeginMatcher explicitly to stop keys with leading bytes being misread as HMAC secrets, and added asymmetric-JWK refusal for the same 'asymmetric key treated as secret' flaw (GHSA-ww5h-9m49-7xx4 / GHSA-g3jj-5cmm-3hxx lineage).

review_queue.evidence: Algorithm-family fallback in the HMAC-confusion family; not reproduced this round.

finding.title: Empty configured key skips signature verification and accepts unsigned tokens
finding.evidence: verifyToken derives hasKey from the key (src/verifier.js:180): for a non-Buffer key it uses `!!key`, so key === '' yields hasKey === false. The guard at lines 182-186 only throws missingSignature when `hasKey && !signature` and missingKey when `!hasKey && signature`; for an attacker-supplied unsigned token of the form `<header>.<payload>.` the decoder returns signature = '' (src/decoder.js:15-16,44), so signature is falsy and neither branch fires. validateAlgorithmAndSignature then checks only the allowlist (line 134) and the actual signature check at line 139 is guarded by `if (signature && !verifySignature(...))`; with signature === '' the whole verification is skipped. Consequently `createVerifier({ key: '', algorithms: ['HS256'] })(unsignedToken)` returns the attacker-chosen payload without any signature verification, an authentication bypass. The later release added ensureSecretIsNotEmpty (rejecting empty string/buffer keys) in both signer and verifier precisely because an HMAC over an empty key authenticates nothing and the empty-signature path bypasses verification.

review_queue.evidence: The canonical null-key empty-signature sink, verified by round4-jwt-verification.json; distinct when another case is labeled.

finding.title: Unvalidated Blake2b key length causes stack buffer overflow in crypto_blake2b_keyed_init
finding.evidence: blake2b(msg, key=None) (line 281) and Blake2b.__init__ (line 297) forward the caller-supplied key and len(key) directly to the C sink crypto_blake2b_keyed_init without any upper-bound check on key length (only _validate_u32 exists for argon2 fields, and it is not applied here). In the reachable C code, monocypher.c:544-549 executes `u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);` where key_size is the unvalidated Python len(key). Any key longer than 128 bytes (e.g. blake2b(b'msg', key=b'A'*256) or Blake2b(key=b'A'*256)) makes COPY write key_size bytes into the 128-byte stack buffer, a classic stack overflow whose contents/length are fully attacker-controlled. No length check exists in either the .pyx wrapper or the C init routine, so the unsafe write is directly reachable with attacker input.

review_queue.evidence: blake2b passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed; monocypher.c copies key_size bytes into key_block[128]. Keys >128 bytes overflow the stack. Source-verified; remote reachability is not claimed.

finding.title: argon2i_32 under-allocates work_area from unvalidated nb_blocks
finding.evidence: argon2i_32(nb_blocks, ...) casts the caller's nb_blocks to size_t and allocates `work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * 1024)` (line 345) without applying _validate_u32 or a minimum-bound check to nb_blocks. crypto_argon2 (monocypher.c:747) computes `segment_size = nb_blocks / nb_lanes / 4; lane_size = segment_size * 4;` with nb_lanes hardcoded to 1, and then, before the main passes, writes two 1024-byte blocks per lane (`// fill first 2 blocks of each lane`, i.e. blocks[0] and blocks[1]). When the caller passes a small nb_blocks (e.g. 1), lane_size becomes 0, so the routine still writes block[1] 1024 bytes past the malloc(nb_blocks*1024) allocation, corrupting adjacent heap memory. Additionally, no NULL check is performed on the malloc result, so a very large nb_blocks yields NULL and crypto_argon2 immediately dereferences/writes it. The wrapper neither validates nb_blocks nor guards the allocation, making the corrupting write reachable with attacker-controlled input.

review_queue.evidence: Unvalidated nb_blocks sizes the work area while native Argon2 reads initialized blocks; same expected undersized-work-area root cause with an alternate CWE at the expected line.

finding.title: ChunkedReader does not validate the CRLF chunk terminator, allowing HTTP request smuggling
finding.evidence:
Attacker-controlled HTTP body bytes reach ChunkedReader (h11/_readers.py:148), selected by READERS[SEND_BODY]['chunked'] for any request/response with Transfer-Encoding: chunked. Input flows: buf.maybe_extract_next_line() -> validate(chunk_header_re,...) parses only the hex chunk-size/extensions line (lines 174-184), then buf.maybe_extract_at_most(self._bytes_in_chunk) consumes the chunk data (line 192) and sets self._bytes_to_discard = 2 (line 197). On the next call, the code at lines 163-170 does `data = buf.maybe_extract_at_most(self._bytes_to_discard)` and simply does `self._bytes_to_discard -= len(data)` (line 167) without checking that the discarded bytes are actually the mandatory b'
' chunk footer. Any two attacker-supplied bytes (e.g. '
X', or any arbitrary/whitespace bytes) are silently accepted as the chunk terminator, so non-conforming chunked framing is treated as valid; only the header line regex (chunk_header_re) guards framing and there is no check of the body terminator. The upstream-fixed 0.16.0 code instead initializes self._bytes_to_discard = b'
' and raises LocalProtocolError('malformed chunk footer') when data != self._bytes_to_discard[:len(data)] (lines 151-174 there), and the changelog/changes.rst Security fix section states these previously-accepted malformed chunked bodies 'could have enabled request-smuggling attacks when an h11-based HTTP server was placed behind a load balancer with a matching bug in its chunked handling'. Locally reproduced against the identical 0.14.0 code: payload b'POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

5
hello
X0

GET /smuggled HTTP/1.1
Host: x

' fed to h11.Connection(h11.SERVER).next_event() yields Request(POST, Transfer-Encoding: chunked), Data(b'hello'), then EndOfMessage with no RemoteProtocolError, while the same reader in 0.16.0 raises 'malformed chunk footer'. Consequences: when h11 parses a chunked body framed differently than an intermediary/proxy (front-end uses strict CRLF, h11 tolerates arbitrary/LF terminators), the message boundary is desynchronized and a second request embedded in the body ('GET /smuggled') is processed or re-routed by the next hop, violating integrity, confidentiality and authorization of the HTTP pipeline. Required configuration is only that h11 run as a server behind a proxy/load balancer that terminates chunked framing, i.e. the standard deployment the advisory targets; no local privileges are needed and the malicious request arrives over the network.

review_queue.evidence: The chunked reader discards the footer/terminator bytes without CRLF validation. Same framing root cause as the expected line-197 sink.

finding.title: UnixFileLock follows attacker-planted symlinks and truncates the resolved target file
finding.evidence: Attacker input is the lock path used to build a UnixFileLock (filelock/__init__.py:38 selects UnixFileLock on POSIX when fcntl is present). In UnixFileLock._acquire the path is passed straight to os.open (filelock/_unix.py:44) with open_flags set at line 41 as os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (with O_CREAT added when Path(self.lock_file).exists() is false, lines 42-43). os.open follows symlinks and O_TRUNC zeroes the file the path resolves to while also returning a writable descriptor, so if an attacker can pre-create the lock path as a symlink to a victim file the locking process can write, acquiring the lock silently truncates that victim file (integrity/availability violation) - for example a privileged process using a lock file inside a shared or world-writable directory. The existing guards do not prevent this: ensure_directory_exists (filelock/_util.py:39-46) only mkdirs the symlink's parent, the Path(...).exists() check at _unix.py:42 itself follows the link, and there is no os.O_NOFOLLOW, no lstat/fstat regular-file validation, and no check that the opened fd still matches the intended path. The async variant inherits the same behavior (filelock/asyncio.py:330 reuses UnixFileLock._acquire). PoC could not be executed on the audit host because it is Windows (sys.platform != POSIX, UnixFileLock._acquire raises NotImplementedError), so this is supported by direct inspection of the reachable POSIX code path rather than local execution.

review_queue.evidence: os.open at line 44 follows the attacker-controlled lock path with O_TRUNC set at line 41 and no O_NOFOLLOW; same protected-file truncation root cause one line after the expected sink. Directory write access and victim write permission are prerequisites.

finding.title: Empty/null key disables signature verification, accepting forged unsigned tokens
finding.evidence: createVerifier validates only the key TYPE (lines 391-397); `key: ''` and `key: null` both pass (`typeof null === 'object'`). Because the key is falsy, the `if (key && keyType !== 'function')` block at line 399 is skipped, so an explicitly supplied `algorithms` allowlist (e.g. ['HS256']) is retained while the key stays empty/falsy. At verify time verifyToken computes `hasKey = key instanceof Buffer ? key.length : !!key` (line 180) = false, so the missing-signature guard `if (hasKey && !signature)` (line 182) is skipped, and `else if (!hasKey && signature)` (line 184) is also false because the attacker leaves the signature segment empty. validateAlgorithmAndSignature then executes `if (signature && !verifySignature(header.alg, key, input, signature))` (line 139) with `signature === ''` (falsy), so no signature check ever runs; only the attacker-controlled `header.alg` is checked against the allowlist. An attacker sends `base64url({"alg":"HS256"}).base64url({"sub":"admin"}).` — the algorithm is allowed, verification is skipped, and the payload is returned as valid, giving a complete authentication bypass whenever a verifier is built with an empty or null key (e.g. `key: process.env.JWT_SECRET` unset).

review_queue.evidence: The canonical null-key empty-signature sink, verified by round4-jwt-verification.json; distinct when another case is labeled.

finding.title: Algorithm confusion: asymmetric PEM/JWK public key misclassified as HMAC secret
finding.evidence: Reached from verifier.js line 401 (`detectPublicKeyAlgorithms(key)`) and line 342 in the async key path. performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms matches the public-key header with the `^`-anchored regex `publicKeyPemMatcher` (crypto.js line 27, `/^-----BEGIN(?: (RSA))? PUBLIC KEY-----/`), so if the developer-supplied public key or X.509 certificate string begins with any byte before `-----BEGIN...` (leading whitespace/newline, a BOM/control character, zero-width character, wrapper text), `key.match(publicKeyPemMatcher)` at line 126 returns null. A serialized asymmetric JWK/JWKS JSON has no PEM header at all and behaves the same. The fallthrough at line 133 (`else if (!publicKeyPemMatch && !key.includes(publicKeyX509CertMatcher)) return hsAlgorithms`) therefore classifies this asymmetric public key as a raw HMAC secret. createVerifier then adopts `hsAlgorithms` as the allowlist and prepareKeyOrSecret (line 409) builds an HMAC secret key directly from the public PEM/JSON string. Because the public key is, by definition, public, an attacker who knows it computes HMAC-SHA256 over `base64url(header).base64url(payload)` using that exact string as the HMAC key, sets `alg=HS256`, and verifySignature accepts the forged token — an algorithm-confusion authentication bypass (CVE-2023-48223 lineage).

review_queue.evidence: Claimed HS256 algorithm confusion when PEM key material is not matched at offset 0. The detection path and a working forgery were not reproduced; keep unreviewed.

finding.title: Double-drop / use-after-free in ThinVec::clear when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: `clear()` calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` (line 1084) over the `len` elements and only resets the length on the next line, `self.set_len(0)` (line 1085). The prefix guarding the length is not installed before the potentially-panicking drop: if any element's `Drop::drop` panics (a safe, attacker-influenceable operation for user types), `drop_in_place` unwinds before `set_len(0)` runs, so the vector keeps its old non-zero length while a prefix of its elements has already been dropped. Because the length was not decremented before each drop (in contrast to the guarded `truncate`, lines 1055-1065, which sets the length before each `drop_in_place`), the still-live `ThinVec` then double-drops those already-dropped elements when it is later dropped, re-cleared, or otherwise accessed. The upstream project's release notes for 0.2.16 explicitly list 'Fix two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() and ThinVec::into_iter() when the Drop implementation of the item panics', and 0.2.21 replaces this body with a `DropGuard` that calls `set_len(0)` on unwind (crates.io thin-vec-0.2.21 `clear`); this 0.2.15 body has no such guard. Attacker prerequisite: code using ThinVec whose element type has a Drop impl that can panic during panic-unwind (e.g. attacker-choosable data driving a panic in Drop). Required configuration: any of the default/std/gecko-ffi feature sets (clear is unconditional).

review_queue.evidence: clear drops its slice at 1084 before setting len to zero at 1085, so a destructor panic leaves a stale live length that a later drop re-drops. reference/FIX.md independently patches this path; distinct from IntoIter cleanup.

finding.title: Double-drop / use-after-free in IntoIter::drop when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: `IntoIter::drop` -> `drop_non_singleton` (line 2547) executes `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` and only afterwards clears the length via `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548). No unwind guard decrements/marks the length before or during the drop. If a remaining element's `Drop::drop` panics, the unwind skips `set_len_non_singleton(0)`; the vector portion whose elements were already dropped retains a non-zero length, so the elements are dropped a second time on subsequent drop/access (double-drop) and the stale length can drive out-of-bounds / use-after-free reads or writes of the moved-from elements. Upstream fixed this exact path in 0.2.16 ('two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() and ThinVec::into_iter() when the Drop implementation of the item panics'); 0.2.21 wraps the `drop_in_place` in a `DropGuard` whose Drop calls `self.0.vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (crates.io thin-vec-0.2.21 `IntoIter::drop`), whereas this 0.2.15 body has no guard. Attacker prerequisite: element type with a Drop impl that panics during iteration/drop. Required configuration: default features. Note: local PoC could not be executed because the crate failed to link on this host (MSVC `link.exe` toolchain error), so the conclusion rests on the inspected source and the upstream fix diff.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: ItemAtIndex index is not range-constrained, allowing out-of-bounds selection
finding.evidence: The SHA256 general/partial selectors take paddedInLength (sender-controlled) and build the selector index inBlockIndex-1 (sha.circom:110-111, 195). ItemAtIndex's only range check is `component lessThan = LessThan(bitLength); lessThan.in[0] <== index; lessThan.in[1] <== maxArrayLen; lessThan.out === 1;` (array.circom:25-28). LessThan is only sound when BOTH operands fit in bitLength bits, but index is never constrained with Num2Bits to bitLength bits. A prover can therefore pass paddedInLength = 0 (or 512*(1-k) so that inBlockIndex = 1-k, i.e. index = -k for small k), which is congruent to a huge field element p-k that LessThan treats as smaller than maxArrayLen and returns 1 for, satisfying the check. Every eqs[i].out then equals 0, so calcTotal.sum = 0 and out <== 0 for all 256 bits. The result is a valid proof that the SHA256 output is all-zeros irrespective of the actual message, breaking the hash binding the circuit is supposed to provide. The `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` constraint (sha.circom:111) does not prevent this because it only forces a multiple of 512, not a bounded non-negative value. The relevant comment in sha.circom:113-122 admits the floor-range checks were left commented out.

review_queue.evidence: ItemAtIndex LessThan guard; same comparator/selector soundness root cause.

finding.title: paddedInLength and derived inBlockIndex lack bit-width constraints in SHA256 templates
finding.evidence: In both Sha256General and Sha256Partial the attacker-supplied paddedInLength is connected to the unconstrained witness `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9); paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512;` (sha.circom:110-111 and 233-234) and is then used in a range comparison `component bitLengthVerifier = LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits); bitLengthVerifier.in[0] <== paddedInLength; bitLengthVerifier.in[1] <== maxBitLength; bitLengthVerifier.out === 1;` (sha.circom:125-128 and 237-240). Because paddedInLength is never constrained with Num2Bits to ceil(log2(maxBitLength)) bits, negative values such as -1 or -512 pass the LessEqThan check and satisfy the multiple-of-512 equality, giving inBlockIndex in {-5,...,0}. That value is then fed as `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (sha.circom:195 and 292), which drives the out-of-bounds ItemAtIndex behavior above and yields an arbitrary (e.g. all-zero) 256-bit output. This upstream class of issue was fixed by adding Num2Bits range constraints on paddedInLength and by replacing the ItemAtIndex LessThan check with an assertion that the selection sum equals 1 (see upstream array.circom, which adds `calcTotalIndex.sum === 1`); this target retains the unconstrained version, so a prover can force the SHA256 circuit to output attacker-chosen bits for any input.

review_queue.evidence: Unbounded inBlockIndex derivation; same comparator/length root cause as the expected sink.

finding.title: ChunkedReader accepts non-CRLF chunk footers, enabling HTTP request smuggling
finding.evidence:
ChunkedReader.__call__ reads chunk data and, when a chunk is exhausted, sets self._bytes_to_discard = 2 (line 197) to consume the trailing CRLF. Lines 163-170 then blindly take those two bytes via buf.maybe_extract_at_most(self._bytes_to_discard) and decrement the counter without ever verifying that the consumed bytes actually equal b"
". Any two attacker-chosen bytes are therefore accepted as the chunk terminator. A remote peer controls the request/response framing (chunk sizes and chunk bodies) when a chunked-coded message is parsed, so it can supply a footer that is not CRLF. Verified against the audited source (h11 0.14.0) with a local PoC: the body 'POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

4
Wiki

0

' is accepted (chunk footer '

'), and '4
WikiXX3
abc
0

' is also accepted with footer 'XX' plus a further chunk ('abc'), producing EndOfMessage. A compliant strict parser (and the fixed h11 0.16.0, which compares data against b"
") rejects these. Because lenient h11 disagrees with compliant intermediaries about chunk boundaries, a front-end/back-end HTTP desync (request smuggling) results: bytes the peer intends as the next request can be interpreted by h11 as chunk data/footer, or vice versa. No configuration or privilege beyond the ability to send a chunked-coded message is required.

review_queue.evidence: The _bytes_to_discard branch consumes the unvalidated chunk footer; same framing root cause as the expected line-197 sink.

finding.title: Unvalidated BLAKE2b key length causes stack buffer overflow
finding.evidence: blake2b() accepts an arbitrary `key` and does no length check (key = b'' if key is None at line 277, then crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), msg, len(msg)) at line 281 passes len(key) straight to C). The same unvalidated length is used by Blake2b.__init__ (self._hash_size = ... at line 296, crypto_blake2b_keyed_init(&self._ctx, self._hash_size, key, len(key)) at line 297). In monocypher.c crypto_blake2b_keyed_init (line 530) the key is copied with `u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);` (lines 545-546), where COPY is an unbounded element-wise loop, so any key_size > 128 writes attacker-controlled bytes past key_block on the stack; no bound is enforced anywhere between the Python argument and the C COPY. Attacker prerequisite: supplying the `key` argument (e.g. an HMAC-style usage where the caller forwards a user/attacker-provided key) with >128 bytes. Demonstrated locally against the 4.0.2.6 build: blake2b(b'msg', b'A'*129) terminates the process (exit 127, native crash from the overflow) and Blake2b(key=b'A'*200) likewise crashes, while a 32-byte key control returns normally. The later 4.0.3.4 wheel rejects these inputs with 'Invalid key length 129 > 64', confirming the missing check is the root cause.

review_queue.evidence: blake2b passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed, whose native copy fills key_block[128]; a long key overflows the stack. Same genuine wrapper defect as line 281 CWE-121, distinct from the expected argon2 work-area issue.

finding.title: Missing length validation of fixed-size key/nonce/mac parameters enables out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: Several wrappers forward caller-supplied buffers to C functions whose signatures declare fixed array sizes (const uint8_t key[32], nonce[24], mac[16], signature[64], public_key[32]), but the Python layer never validates the lengths. lock() (line 181) passes key/nonce straight to crypto_aead_lock; unlock() (line 199) passes mac/key/nonce to crypto_aead_unlock; IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption.__init__ only checks the nonce (lines 214-220) but passes key to crypto_aead_init_x without checking key length; chacha20() (lines 267/269) passes key to crypto_chacha20_x/djb; signature_check() (line 429) passes signature/public_key to crypto_eddsa_check; key_exchange() (line 375) passes your_secret_key/their_public_key to crypto_x25519. In Cython the `[32]`/`[24]` array-size annotations decay to plain pointers and are NOT enforced at runtime (only a compile-time warning is emitted), so the C code reads 32/24/64 bytes regardless of the actual object size. A short bytes object yields an out-of-bounds read of adjacent heap memory (potential disclosure or crash). Demonstrated locally against the 4.0.2.6 build: lock(b'A'*1, b'N'*24, b'msg'), lock(b'K'*32, b'N'*1, b'msg'), unlock(b'K'*32, b'N'*24, b'M'*1, b'ct'), chacha20(b'A'*1, b'N'*8, b'msg'), signature_check(b's'*1, b'p'*32, b'msg'), signature_check(b's'*64, b'p'*1, b'msg') and key_exchange(b'A'*1, b'B'*1) all execute without any length error, silently reading past the supplied buffers, whereas the 4.0.3.4 wheel rejects over-length keys, confirming validation is the missing protection.

review_queue.evidence: lock()/unlock() pass caller-controlled key and nonce buffers into native routines declaring key[32]/nonce[24] without a length check; the incremental wrapper guards lengths at lines 214-218. Distinct AEAD bounds defect; no native crash or disclosure reproduced.

finding.title: Unvalidated BLAKE2b key length overflows 128-byte stack buffer
finding.evidence: blake2b() accepts an attacker-controlled `key` and forwards its raw length with no bounds check: `key = b'' if key is None else key` then `crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), msg, len(msg))` (c_monocypher.pyx:277-281). The Blake2b class does the same at line 297 (`crypto_blake2b_keyed_init(&self._ctx, self._hash_size, key, len(key))`). In monocypher.c the keyed init performs an unbounded copy `u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);` (monocypher.c:547-548), where COPY is a raw byte-copy macro and key_size is the caller-supplied length. There is no `len(key)` validation in the .pyx (unlike IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption which enforces length 32). A call such as `monocypher.blake2b(b'msg', key=b'A'*300)` writes 300 bytes into the 128-byte stack buffer key_block, a stack buffer overflow that corrupts adjacent stack memory (saved registers/return address), reachable from a single public Python API call.

review_queue.evidence: blake2b passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed, whose native copy fills key_block[128]; a long key overflows the stack. Same genuine wrapper defect as line 281 CWE-121, distinct from the expected argon2 work-area issue.

finding.title: Unchecked malloc result fed to crypto_argon2 in argon2i_32
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 takes caller-controlled `nb_blocks` and passes it to an unchecked allocation: `work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * (<size_t> 1024))` (c_monocypher.pyx:345), and then unconditionally calls `crypto_argon2(hash, <uint32_t> len(hash), work_area, config, inputs, extras)` (line 347). The malloc return value is never checked for NULL, and `nb_blocks` is only constrained by the uint32 struct field (values up to 0xffff_ffff are accepted; only >2^32 raises). In monocypher.c the pointer is immediately dereferenced and written: `blk *blocks = (blk*)work_area;` (monocypher.c:757) followed by block writes (monocypher.c:781). Supplying a large value such as `argon2i_32(0xfffffff, 1, b'p', b's')` makes malloc fail and return NULL, causing a NULL-pointer write/crash inside the native library; the `finally: free(work_area)` cannot prevent it, yielding denial of service when callers forward untrusted KDF parameters.

review_queue.evidence: crypto_argon2 consumes the malloc result without a NULL check; distinct allocation-failure path from undersized work area.

finding.title: Unconstrained paddedInLength lets prover force SHA256 output to zero (soundness break)
finding.evidence: paddedInLength is an unconstrained prover-supplied input signal. It is only tied to witness-computed inBlockIndex via `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)` (l.110) and `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (l.111). No constraint bounds paddedInLength to the non-negative integer range [0, maxBitLength] with the required bit width; the only length guard is `LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits)` (l.125-128), and circomlib LessEqThan does not range-check its operands (it only decomposes `in[0]+2^n-in[1]`), so field elements such as 0 or -512 (== p-512) satisfy it. Choosing paddedInLength = 0 (e.g. Sha256Bytes.paddedInLength=0, or a small negative passed to Sha256Bytes since it multiplies by 8) yields inBlockIndex=0; then `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (l.195, duplicated at l.292 in Sha256Partial) becomes -1 == p-1. ItemAtIndex accepts this out-of-range index (array.circom:25-28 do not constrain index to bitLength bits; LessThan(bitLength) returns 1 for p-1 because p-1+2^n-maxArrayLen < 2^n), while every IsEqual against i in [0,maxBlocks) fails, so out = sum = 0 for all 256 bits. A malicious prover can therefore prove SHA256(arbitrary bytes) = 0 (all-zero hash) for any paddedIn, breaking the soundness of Sha256Bytes/Sha256BytesPartial; the same path applies to Sha256Partial at l.233-234 and l.292.

review_queue.evidence: Unbounded paddedInLength equality; same comparator/length root cause.

finding.title: ItemAtIndex bounds check bypassable via unconstrained index (QuinSelector returns 0)
finding.evidence: ItemAtIndex enforces its bounds check with `LessThan(bitLength)` fed directly by the attacker-controlled signal `index` (l.25-28) without first constraining index to bitLength bits. circomlib LessThan only decomposes `index + 2^bitLength - maxArrayLen` into bitLength+1 bits and tests the top bit; it never range-checks index, so a value such as -1 (== p-1) makes the sum small and `lessThan.out === 1` passes even though index >= maxArrayLen. Because the equality terms all fail, `calcTotal.sum` (l.41-45) is 0 and out is 0. This is reachable from Sha256General/Sha256Partial (sha.circom:191-196 and 288-293), where `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` can be driven to p-1 by an attacker-chosen paddedInLength that is not range-constrained, letting a prover obtain an all-zero SHA256 output for arbitrary input. Fixing either the caller's length range check or this comparison removes the exploit; both defects are required for the reported zero-hash forgery.

review_queue.evidence: ItemAtIndex selector comparison; same comparator/selector soundness root cause.

finding.title: inBlockIndex-1 underflow bypasses ItemAtIndex bounds check and forces all-zero hash output
finding.evidence: Input: paddedInLength is a free prover signal. Flow: line 111 `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` constrains inBlockIndex = paddedInLength/512 and permits the value 0 (the only guard is bitLengthVerifier at lines 125-128, and `0 <= maxBitLength`, so paddedInLength=0 is accepted). Line 195 then computes `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1`, which for inBlockIndex=0 evaluates to -1 mod p = p-1 (the BN254 scalar prime), an out-of-range array index. Failed protection: ItemAtIndex (array.circom lines 15-46) is supposed to reject this via `LessThan(bitLength).in[0] <== index; in[1] <== maxArrayLen; out === 1`, but circomlib's LessThan computes `Num2Bits(n+1)` on `in[0]+2^n-in[1]` and does not range-check its inputs; with index=p-1 the value wraps to `2^n - maxArrayLen - 1` (e.g. 1 for maxArrayLen=2), whose top bit is 0, so LessThan returns 1. I reproduced this in Node against the BN254 prime for maxArrayLen in {1,2,4,16}: LessThan.out=1 for index=p-1, i.e. the bounds check is bypassed. Unsafe operation: because no eqs[i].in[1] (= index = p-1) equals any i in [0,maxArrayLen), every IsEqual outputs 0, CalculateTotal.sum=0, and line 196 `out[k] <== arraySelectors[k].out` is forced to 0. Consequence: for arbitrary paddedIn bits and paddedInLength=0, the prover can generate a valid proof whose 256-bit output is all zeros, a false SHA-256 statement (real SHA-256 never yields 0), i.e. a soundness break. The same pattern repeats at line 292 in Sha256Partial and is reached from Sha256Bytes (line 33) / Sha256BytesPartial (line 65). Required configuration: any instantiation (e.g. Sha256Bytes(64) => maxBitLength=512, maxBlocks=1).

review_queue.evidence: Sha256General/Sha256Partial derive inBlockIndex from an unbounded paddedInLength and feed inBlockIndex-1 into ItemAtIndex, whose LessThan lacks a range check. Same comparator/selector soundness defect as the expected line-126 sink.
